stem: In which direction does the resultant force on an object moving in a circle at constant speed act?

options.content: Towards the centre of the circle

options.rationale: The direction keeps changing, so there must be one.

explanation: The centripetal (resultant) force acts towards the centre, at right angles to the motion.

stem: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string. What provides the force towards the centre?

options.rationale: Air resistance opposes motion along the path.

explanation: The string pulls the stone inwards: tension provides the centripetal force.

stem: What provides the centripetal force for the Moon orbiting the Earth?

options.content: The gravitational pull of the Earth

options.rationale: There is almost no air in space.

explanation: The Earth's gravitational attraction pulls the Moon towards the centre of its orbit.

stem: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle and the string breaks. How does the stone move immediately afterwards (seen from above)?

options.content: Straight outwards, away from the centre
It keeps going round the circle
options.rationale: Without the inward force it cannot.

options.content: In a straight line along the tangent to the circle
options.rationale: Correct: no resultant force, so it moves in a straight line.

explanation: With the inward force gone, the stone carries on in a straight line in the direction it was moving at that instant: along the tangent.
hints: Newton's first law: what happens with no resultant force?

stem: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating.
explanation: Its direction, and so its velocity, keeps changing; the acceleration is towards the centre.

stem: A car goes round the same bend twice, the second time at a higher speed. What happens to the friction force needed to keep it on the bend?

options.rationale: Correct: a larger speed needs a larger centripetal force.
Some force is always needed to turn.

explanation: With the same mass and radius, a larger speed needs a larger force towards the centre.
hints: Mass and radius stay the same; only the speed changes.

stem: A girl whirls a ball on a string at a steady speed, then pulls the string harder while keeping the speed the same. What happens to the circle?

options.rationale: More inward force pulls it into a smaller circle.
Correct: more force at the same speed and mass gives a tighter circle.
Its speed is kept the same.

explanation: With mass and speed constant, increasing the centripetal force decreases the radius.
hints: Speed and mass are kept constant.

stem: Match each circular motion with the force that keeps it moving in a circle.

left.content: A car going round a roundabout
A conker whirled on a string
An electron orbiting a nucleus (simple model)

explanation: Different forces can provide the centripetal force; it always acts towards the centre.

stem: A loaded truck and an empty truck take the same bend at the same speed. Which needs the larger centripetal force?

options.rationale: Correct: larger mass needs a larger force.

explanation: With speed and radius the same, the force needed increases with mass.
hints: Which quantity is different between the two trucks?

stem: What name is given to the resultant force towards the centre that keeps an object moving in a circle?
explanation: It is the centripetal force (centripetal means 'centre-seeking').

stem: A minibus takes a sharp bend on a gravel road.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why there must be a resultant force on the minibus as it goes round the bend at a constant speed.

points.description: Its direction of motion is changing, so its velocity is changing (it is accelerating)
A change in velocity needs a resultant force, which acts towards the centre of the bend

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which force provides this resultant force?

options.rationale: Air resistance acts against the motion.

options.content: Friction between the tyres and the road

parts.explanation: Sideways friction on the tyres pushes the minibus towards the centre of the bend.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why the minibus may skid if the driver takes the bend too fast on loose gravel.

points.description: A higher speed needs a larger centripetal (friction) force
Loose gravel can provide only a small friction force, so it is not enough and the minibus slides off in a straighter line (outwards from the curve)

explanation: Changing direction means accelerating, which needs an inward resultant force: tyre friction. Faster needs more friction than loose gravel can give, so the minibus skids.
hints: Gravel gives less grip than tar.

stem: A passenger in a minibus going round a bend says, 'I am thrown outwards by a force pushing me away from the centre.' Which is the best explanation?

options.content: An outward centrifugal force pushes her.
options.rationale: No real outward force acts on her.

options.content: Her weight increases on the bend.
Her body tends to keep moving in a straight line (inertia) while the minibus turns towards the centre.

explanation: She keeps going straight until the door or seat pushes her inwards; the minibus turns under her, so she seems to be thrown outwards.
